Use medical evidence on transmission and vaccine effectiveness to determine required coverage, applicable legal provisions to determine permissible charges and exemptions, and integer optimization with public-finance budgeting to determine the subsidy. Assume homogeneous mixing, no prior immunity, identical eligibility, population N, per-person vaccination cost c, and legal provisions yielding a fee cap f<c and P nonexempt residents; select supported parameters so both coverage calculations require exempt recipients, the correct unrounded requirement is nonintegral, and all five subsidy results are distinct.
fusion_idea.correct_answer_plan: Under an appropriate vaccine-effectiveness model and the criterion R_eff≤1, derive K=ceil[N(1−1/R0)/e], then minimize the tax subsidy by vaccinating all P nonexempt residents at the lawful maximum fee and K−P exempt residents without charge. With medical coverage and integer optimization otherwise correct, eliminating fee revenue produces the unnecessarily large subsidy cK.

Treat vaccination as certain protection rather than accounting for imperfect effectiveness, producing K0=ceil[N(1−1/R0)]. Correct legal charging and financial optimization then yield cK0−fP; choose K0≤K−2 to distinguish this from the rounding distractor.

Read the general charging authority as applying to every recipient and overlook the applicable income-based exemption. With the correct medical target and optimization, charging all K recipients the cap produces the unlawfully low subsidy (c−f)K.

fusion_idea.idea: Plan a five-option question asking which government flood-protection package and uniform levy rate provide the least-cost lawful solution, retaining the source distinction that collective, nondiscriminatory public needs do not imply zero-price financing. Geography establishes hydrologically connected communities and downstream effects; legal rules determine protection duties, levy exemptions and a rate ceiling; financial knowledge connects collective provision to funding, while mathematics optimizes indivisible, overlapping investments. Supply hypothetical statutory extracts, hydrological data, project costs and assessed values, with levy revenue as the sole funding source; require a unique optimum, a positive exempt assessment base, protection regardless of exemption, and parameters making all four diagnostic alternatives distinct.
fusion_idea.correct_answer_plan: Determine protection requirements across the connected area, including downstream communities, and minimize project cost subject to those requirements and the lawful funding ceiling. Apply the prescribed uniform levy to the nonexempt assessment base, yielding the optimal package and its cost divided by that base.

distractor_plans.plan: Mistake collective public benefit for a requirement that beneficiaries pay nothing, rejecting even an authorized levy. With geography, legal permissions and optimization otherwise understood, conclude that no fundable solution exists because other revenue sources are unavailable.

Treat an administrative boundary as a hydrological boundary and omit a downstream, levy-exempt community despite its hydraulic connection. Correctly applying financing, law and optimization to this mistaken protection footprint produces a cheaper, incomplete package and its lower levy rate.

Assume that receiving flood protection automatically makes a community liable for the levy, overlooking the statutory exemption. Using the correct hydrology, optimal infrastructure and financing arithmetic produces the correct package paired with an unlawfully low rate calculated over an enlarged assessment base.

Use greedy standalone protection-per-cost rankings rather than optimizing indivisible projects with overlapping coverage. With hydrology, legal constraints and revenue calculations correct, select a fully protective but strictly more expensive package and its higher lawful levy rate; choose parameters ensuring this package remains within the ceiling.

fusion_idea.idea: Plan a five-option question asking which drinking-water safety program minimizes general-tax subsidy while protecting the population and satisfying applicable law, retaining the source distinction that meeting shared public needs does not necessarily require price-free provision. Use microbial and nitrate contamination, infant exposure, treatment-performance data, and a jurisdiction-specific tariff framework: medical knowledge identifies protection needs, chemistry evaluates contaminant removal and by-products, legal knowledge determines permissible charges, and financial knowledge distinguishes public provision from mandatory free access. Retrieve supporting clinical and treatment evidence, and specify costs, tariff-authorization facts, and access safeguards so that one compliant, protective program uniquely minimizes subsidy without over-recovering costs.
fusion_idea.correct_answer_plan: Select validated nitrate removal plus effective disinfection with acceptable by-products, financed through an authorized tariff with access safeguards and a residual tax subsidy. Establish that this meets population-health requirements and needs less tax support than an otherwise identical free-at-use program.

distractor_plans.plan: Mistaking shared public needs for services that must be free at use causes rejection of any user tariff and selection of the fully tax-funded treatment program. Medical protection, treatment chemistry, and legal permissibility are correctly assessed, but the program unnecessarily increases the required tax subsidy.

Failing to recognize infants' susceptibility to nitrate-associated methemoglobinemia makes microbial control alone appear sufficient, producing selection of a cheaper disinfection-only program. Treatment chemistry correctly establishes that nitrate remains, and financing and tariff law are correctly applied, but its clinical significance is missed.

Assuming household boiling removes dissolved nitrate makes a disinfection-plus-boiling program appear to provide the required protection at lower cost than validated nitrate removal. Infant nitrate risk, public-service financing, and tariff law are correctly understood, but boiling does not remove nitrate and can concentrate it.

Treating a utility's general revenue-raising power as sufficient authority for an unapproved higher tariff leads to selection of validated treatment financed by that tariff, apparently requiring the least subsidy. Medical protection, chemical performance, and the financial legitimacy of charging for public services are correctly understood, but the applicable authorization requirement is missed.
